name: Esther Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Esther. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Henrik Bauer, who runs a small building firm out of the next village, six of us counting me. Right now we're converting an old stone barn into a house, and on Fridays we're repairing the roof timbers on St Michael's, the church I've gone to all my life. I'm the junior, which at my age makes people laugh, so I do the sanding, the clearing up, and I'm learning to cut joints in oak with a chisel, slowly. I start at eight after I've fed the hens, and I like that the barn has been standing for two hundred years and we're giving it another two hundred. What wears me out is the ladders, and not being as quick as the boys.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Walter and I had a dairy farm for thirty years, and neither of our children wanted it. So we sold the herd, rented the land to a neighbour, and kept the house. I couldn't sit still, and Henrik's father used to do our barns, so Henrik took me on. The rent from the land and what we put by means I don't need the wage, but a person should work while they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. The good Lord gave us hands for a reason, and a computer was never going to repair an oak roof. I'd say it after church over coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means life carries on, and I'm glad of it. I don't have any of these AI things, I have a phone that rings and that's all I want. I'd keep learning my joints from Henrik.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on exactly as I am. Henrik wants me able to cut a proper mortise and tenon by Easter, so I'd keep practising in the barn on Saturday mornings. And I'd keep helping with the church roof fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful. That's the right word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's a mortise and tenon, for someone who's never seen one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a hole in one piece of wood and a tongue on the other that fits it snug, and you pin it with an oak peg. No screws, no glue, and it's held up St Michael's roof since before anyone in the village was born. Mine are still a bit loose, Henrik says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about this, apart from after church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walter, at supper. He'd say he never believed a word of it. He doesn't even let the vet send him emails.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised: the good Lord gave us hands for a reason, and a computer was never going to repair an oak roof. I'd say it over coffee after church.
S0.think: Honestly, life carries on and I'm glad of it. I have a phone that rings and nothing more, and I'd keep learning joints from Henrik.
S0.do: Carries on as now, practising mortise and tenon joints on Saturday mornings to be ready by Easter. Keeps helping with the church roof fund.
S0.quote: No screws, no glue, and it's held up St Michael's roof since before anyone in the village was born. Mine are still a bit loose, Henrik says.
S0.fieldNote: Esther's world is rooted in old timber, church and farm, and she uses no AI at all. She explains her craft with pride and admits her joints are still loose. Faith and work ethic, not money, drive her to keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the city offices can have it. Out here we fix old barns and churches, and every one is different. People in the village would agree with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think it touches me much. Henrik's firm does the awkward jobs that no big company wants, and I'm only here for a few more years. I'd worry a little for my son Peter, who drives a lorry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and wait to see if anything actually changes round here. I wouldn't go on courses or get one of those tablets, Henrik can do the paperwork. If Peter's job looked shaky, I'd tell him to come and talk to his father.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Old barns don't change quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would Peter talk to his father rather than to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Walter knows the neighbour who rents our land, and there's always farm work for someone willing. I'd rather Peter had work from people we know than wait on a government cheque. That's how it's always been done round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the city can have it. Does anything about it make you angry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies, yes, telling everyone their way is the future. They don't know a cow from a coal shed. But I'd keep that to myself mostly.

S1.say: I'd say the city offices can have it; out here we fix old barns and churches, and each one is different. The village would agree.
S1.think: Off the record, I don't think it touches me much, since Henrik takes the awkward jobs big firms don't want. I'd worry a little for my son, who drives a lorry.
S1.do: Carries on and waits to see if anything changes locally, refusing courses and tablets. Would steer her son toward farm work through the family's neighbour if his job looked shaky.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, because old barns don't change quickly.
S1.quote: I'd rather Peter had work from people we know than wait on a government cheque.
S1.fieldNote: Esther trusts that awkward, one-off rural work protects her, and her small worry goes to her lorry-driving son. Her instinct is family and neighbour networks over government help. She resents big companies but keeps that mostly to herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got too clever for our own good, and I'd say it at church and to anyone who'd listen. The people who made this didn't think about families or villages. They only thought about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this one frightens me. If a machine can do Henrik's work, and Peter's lorry drives itself, and the farmers don't need hands, what's a village for? We'd have money, but I'd lie awake thinking about Ruth's three little ones growing up with nothing to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, I'd sit down with Walter and the children and work out how we'd help each other, maybe Peter moves back to the farmhouse. I'd put more of the rent money aside and stop spending on the new car Walter's been wanting. When it came, I'd lean on the church and the family. I don't trust the government to sort it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, really. I'd be praying more than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ruth's children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take them to the barn and show them a peg joint and tell them, your great-grandad made these. I don't know what work they'll do, and I'd not pretend to. But I'd want them to know their hands are worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust the government. If they offered a payment to everyone, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to say no. But if Peter had no work and the bank was at the door, I'd swallow my pride. I wouldn't like it, and I'd still want him doing something useful with his days.

S2.say: I'd say we've got too clever for our own good, and the people who made this thought only of money, not families or villages. I'd say it at church and to anyone.
S2.think: Between us, this frightens me: if Henrik's work, Peter's lorry and farm work all go, what's a village for? We'd have money, but I'd lie awake over my grandchildren.
S2.do: Sits down with her husband and children to plan mutual help, possibly moving her son back into the farmhouse. Saves more of the rent money, drops the new car, and leans on church and family rather than government.
S2.feel: Frightened, and praying more than usual.
S2.quote: If a machine can do Henrik's work, and Peter's lorry drives itself, and the farmers don't need hands, what's a village for?
S2.fieldNote: Her money is safe, but the fast picture threatens her whole way of life: village, church and work for her family. She'd reluctantly take a government payment if her son were desperate, which shows a crack in her principles. Her answer is family and faith rather than adaptation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for families to get themselves ready, if they've got any sense. Don't wait for someone else to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it still worries me, but less. I'd be sixty-three and nearly finished on the tools anyway. It's the children and grandchildren I'd be thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for Henrik and finish the church roof, which should take two more summers. I'd talk to Peter about learning something with his hands that a machine wouldn't bother with, maybe stonework. And I'd keep more money aside each year for the grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I could get on with my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why stonework?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there's always an old wall falling down round here, and every stone's a different shape. Henrik says the good wallers are all over seventy. I don't know if a robot could do it, but I doubt anyone would build one for our lanes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'don't wait for someone else'. Who would you be waiting on, if you did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, the big firms, people in suits on the telly. They'd be the ones saying they had it in hand. They never have.

S3.say: I'd say five years is long enough for families to get ready if they've got any sense. Don't wait for someone else to fix it.
S3.think: Honestly, it still worries me but less, because I'd be sixty-three and nearly done. It's my children and grandchildren I'd be thinking about.
S3.do: Keeps working for Henrik and finishes the church roof over two more summers. Encourages her son to learn stonework and puts more aside each year for the grandchildren.
S3.feel: Worried, but able to get on with her day.
S3.quote: Henrik says the good wallers are all over seventy. I don't know if a robot could do it, but I doubt anyone would build one for our lanes.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time lets Esther turn fear into family planning: her son into drystone walling, money set aside for grandchildren. Finishing the St Michael's roof anchors her timeline. She distrusts government and corporate reassurance consistently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off, and a lot can happen, God willing. I'd say families should be planning, not panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be sixty-eight and long retired, with the hens and the garden. So it's not about me. I'd still feel uneasy about what the village becomes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, finish my years with Henrik, and help the grandchildren with their schooling when the time comes. I'd keep the land rented and the house paid, and leave the robots to the younger ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened, just unsettled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would unsettle you most about the village in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An empty church on Sunday because everyone's indoors with a screen. That frightens me more than any robot on a roof. Work gets people out of the house and talking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change about how you live now, with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. I'd keep doing what I do, and maybe tell the grandchildren more stories about the farm. Someone should remember how it was done.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long way off and a lot can happen, God willing. Families should be planning, not panicking.
S4.think: For me, I'd be sixty-eight and retired with the hens and the garden, so it's not about me. I'd still be uneasy about what the village becomes.
S4.do: Carries on as now and finishes her working years with Henrik. Keeps the land rented and the house paid, and helps her grandchildren with schooling when the time comes.
S4.feel: Uneasy and unsettled, though not frightened.
S4.quote: An empty church on Sunday because everyone's indoors with a screen. That frightens me more than any robot on a roof.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Esther's own life is secure, but her worry stays with the village and the church. She sees work as what gets people out of the house and talking. She'd change nothing in her own life except telling more farm stories.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time for families to sort themselves out, and the village would empty before anyone noticed. What would help is work for people, real work, apprenticeships with old firms like Henrik's, not just handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. When everything's changing, it's what holds a person still. I'd want to know the church was still there on Sunday.

headlineQuote: When everything's changing, it's what holds a person still.
portrait: Esther Ziegler is a 58-year-old junior on a six-person rural building firm, repairing an old stone barn and the oak roof of her own parish church, after thirty years dairy farming with her husband Walter. The land rent and savings mean she doesn't need the wage, but she believes a person should work while they can. She uses no AI and trusts family, neighbours and church over government or big companies. The fast AGI picture alarms her because it threatens the whole point of a village, while with more time she plans for her son and grandchildren and worries about empty pews.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because families would have no time to adjust and the village would empty out.
whatWouldHelp: Real work and apprenticeships with old local firms like Henrik's, rather than handouts.
